title: Cellular respiration and photosynthesis
blurb: Trace how cells make ATP from glucose, what happens without oxygen, and how photosynthesis builds glucose from light.
question: During a 400-meter sprint a runner's leg muscles run short of oxygen and start to burn. Where in the muscle cell is ATP still being made, how much, and what by-product builds up? And how does a plant make the glucose that fuels it all?

teach.body: Formal definition: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the molecule cells use to transfer energy; energy is released when its last phosphate bond is hydrolyzed (ATP to ADP + Pi). Aerobic cellular respiration makes ATP: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ to 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy (ATP + heat). Plain English: cells "burn" glucose with oxygen, slowly and in steps, and bank the energy as ATP, breathing out carbon dioxide and making water.

steps.label: Glycolysis
steps.sub: Cytoplasm: glucose to 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP; no O₂ needed

steps.label:
Pyruvate
oxidation
steps.sub: Into the mitochondrial matrix; CO₂ released

steps.label: Krebs cycle
steps.sub: Matrix: releases CO₂; makes NADH and FADH2

steps.label:
Electron
transport chain
steps.sub: Inner membrane (cristae): MOST ATP; O₂ forms water

teach.caption: Total yield is roughly 30–38 ATP per glucose; textbooks vary, so the exam will not hinge on one exact number.

teach.h: Oxygen's one job, and what happens without it
teach.body: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain; it combines with electrons and hydrogen to form water. With no oxygen, the chain and the Krebs cycle stall, and the cell falls back on fermentation: glycolysis alone, giving just 2 ATP per glucose. Human muscle makes lactic acid; yeast makes ethanol and CO₂, which is why bread rises and beer ferments.

Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy to C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. In the light-dependent reactions (thylakoid membranes), chlorophyll captures light, water is split and O₂ is released, and ATP and NADPH are made. The Calvin cycle (light-independent, in the stroma) uses that ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into sugar. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green.

steps.label: ATP + NADPH
steps.sub: Energy carriers pass to the stroma

teach.caption: The two equations are roughly the reverse of each other. Plants do both.

teach.body: Marcus, a pre-nursing student, sprints 400 meters. At first his muscle cells run full aerobic respiration: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, then the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain in the mitochondria, with oxygen accepting electrons to form water. As oxygen runs short, the chain stalls. Glycolysis keeps going in the cytoplasm, giving 2 ATP per glucose, and pyruvate is turned into lactic acid. When he rests and breathes hard, oxygen returns and aerobic respiration resumes.

teach.text: Exam reversals to avoid: the MOST ATP comes from the electron transport chain (not glycolysis or the Krebs cycle); respiration PRODUCES CO₂ and USES O₂, photosynthesis does the opposite; plant cells have mitochondria and respire too; glycolysis needs no oxygen.

items: Respiration: glucose + 6 O₂ to 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + ATP.
Glycolysis (cytoplasm, 2 ATP, no O₂) to Krebs (matrix, CO₂) to ETC (cristae, most ATP).
O₂ is the final electron acceptor and forms water.
No O₂: fermentation, 2 ATP. Muscle: lactic acid. Yeast: ethanol + CO₂.
Photosynthesis: light reactions (thylakoids, O₂ from water) then Calvin cycle (stroma, CO₂ fixed).

summary: You can now put the stages of aerobic respiration in order with their locations and products, explain oxygen's role, and say what fermentation yields in muscle and yeast. You can also describe the two stages of photosynthesis and explain why its equation mirrors respiration.

A.q: Which stage of aerobic cellular respiration produces the most ATP?
A.why: The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane produces most of the ATP from each glucose.

whyNot.0: Glycolysis yields a net of just 2 ATP per glucose.
whyNot.1: The Krebs cycle mainly produces CO₂, NADH and FADH2; it makes little ATP directly.
whyNot.3: Fermentation is anaerobic and yields only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.

A.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does glycolysis take place?
A.why: Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria.

whyNot.1: The matrix is where pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle happen.
whyNot.2: The inner membrane (cristae) holds the electron transport chain.
whyNot.3: Thylakoid membranes are in chloroplasts and host the light reactions of photosynthesis.

A.q: What is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain?
A.why: Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with hydrogen to form water.

whyNot.0: CO₂ is a waste product released earlier, in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle; it accepts no electrons.
whyNot.1: Glucose is the starting fuel, broken down in glycolysis.
whyNot.2: NAD+ picks up electrons earlier (in glycolysis and Krebs) and delivers them TO the chain.

B.q: Which pair of products results from alcoholic fermentation in yeast?
B.why: Yeast fermentation turns pyruvate into ethanol and CO₂; the CO₂ makes bread rise.

whyNot.0: Lactic acid is the product of fermentation in human muscle, not yeast.
whyNot.2: Fermentation happens without oxygen and does not release it.
whyNot.3: Lactic acid fermentation does not produce CO₂, and yeast makes ethanol, not lactic acid.

B.q: The oxygen gas released by a plant during photosynthesis comes from:
options: The Calvin cycle in the stroma
B.why: In the light-dependent reactions, water is split in the thylakoids and its oxygen is released as O₂.

whyNot.1: CO₂ is fixed into sugar in the Calvin cycle; it is not the source of the O₂ released.
whyNot.2: Glucose is a product of photosynthesis, not something broken down to release O₂.
whyNot.3: The Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ into sugar; it does not release oxygen.

B.q: Why do most plant leaves appear green?
options: Chloroplasts absorb red and green light
Chlorophyll reflects red and blue light
B.why: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, so leaves look green.

whyNot.0: Absorbed light is not seen; green is the light chlorophyll does NOT absorb.
whyNot.2: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light; green is reflected.
whyNot.3: Red and blue light are absorbed for photosynthesis, not reflected.

C.q: Which statement comparing photosynthesis and cellular respiration is correct?
options: Respiration releases O₂ and uses CO₂
Plant cells carry out both processes
Animal cells carry out both processes
C.why: Plant cells photosynthesize in chloroplasts and also carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria.

whyNot.0: This is reversed: respiration uses O₂ and releases CO₂.
whyNot.1: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts; mitochondria carry out respiration.
whyNot.3: Animal cells have no chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesize.

C.q: During an all-out sprint, Marcus's leg muscle cells run short of oxygen. Which change takes place in those cells?
options: Pyruvate is converted to ethanol and CO₂
The Krebs cycle speeds up to make more ATP
The ETC keeps running using CO₂ instead
Pyruvate is converted to lactic acid
C.why: Without enough oxygen, human muscle relies on glycolysis plus lactic acid fermentation, which yields 2 ATP per glucose.

whyNot.0: Ethanol and CO₂ are produced by yeast (alcoholic fermentation), not human muscle.
whyNot.1: The Krebs cycle depends on aerobic conditions; it slows when oxygen runs short.
whyNot.2: CO₂ cannot accept electrons; oxygen is the only final acceptor of the chain.

C.q: A cell completely oxidizes 2 molecules of glucose by aerobic respiration. How many molecules of O₂ are used and CO₂ released?
C.why: One glucose + 6 O₂ gives 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O, so 2 glucose use 2 × 6 = 12 O₂ and release 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

whyNot.0: These are the amounts for ONE glucose; the question uses two.
whyNot.2: This is reversed: respiration uses O₂ and releases CO₂ (photosynthesis does the opposite).
whyNot.3: The equation uses 6 O₂ per glucose, so 2 glucose need 12 O₂, not 2.

reteach.title: Cashing a paycheck
reteach.question: Think of glucose as a big paycheck that has to be broken into small bills before you can spend it. How does the cell cash it?

blocks.body: Glucose is a large check: too big to spend directly. Glycolysis is the corner store that cashes a little of it right away (2 ATP), even with no bank open (no oxygen). The Krebs cycle is the teller who processes the rest and fills envelopes (NADH, FADH2). The electron transport chain is the vault that turns those envelopes into most of your cash (ATP), and it only opens when oxygen is there to receive the leftover electrons.

steps.label: Corner store
steps.sub: Glycolysis: net 2 ATP, no O₂ needed

steps.label: Teller
steps.sub: Krebs cycle: fills NADH and FADH2 envelopes

steps.label: Vault
steps.sub: ETC: most of the ATP; opens only with O₂

blocks.text: No oxygen means the vault stays shut: only the corner store pays out, 2 ATP per glucose (fermentation).

explain.body: ATP stores energy in its phosphate bonds; hydrolyzing the last one (ATP to ADP + Pi) releases it. Respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ to 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy.

test.q: Energy stored in ATP is released for cell work when:
options: Its last phosphate bond is hydrolyzed
Its adenine base is split from ribose
A fourth phosphate group is attached
Its sugar is oxidized to carbon dioxide
test.why: Hydrolyzing the terminal phosphate bond (ATP to ADP + Pi) releases usable energy.

whyNot.1: Energy release comes from the phosphate bond, not from separating adenine and ribose.
whyNot.2: ATP has three phosphates; adding phosphate stores energy rather than releasing it.
whyNot.3: Oxidizing sugar is what respiration does to glucose to MAKE ATP, not how ATP releases energy.

explain.body: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP, no O₂ needed. Krebs cycle (matrix): releases CO₂ and loads NADH and FADH2. Electron transport chain (cristae): makes most ATP; O₂ forms water.

test.q: Which stage releases CO₂ in the mitochondrial matrix and produces NADH and FADH2?
test.why: The Krebs (citric acid) cycle runs in the matrix, releases CO₂ and fills the carriers NADH and FADH2.

whyNot.0: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and produces pyruvate, not FADH2.
whyNot.1: The ETC uses NADH and FADH2 to make ATP; it does not release CO₂.
whyNot.3: The Calvin cycle is part of photosynthesis and USES CO₂ in the chloroplast stroma.

explain.body: No O₂ means no electron transport chain. Cells run glycolysis only (2 ATP) and recycle pyruvate by fermentation: lactic acid in human muscle; ethanol and CO₂ in yeast.

test.q: How much ATP does a cell gain per glucose from glycolysis when oxygen is absent?
test.why: Fermentation relies on glycolysis alone, which gives a net of 2 ATP per glucose.

whyNot.0: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2, so the NET gain is 2.
whyNot.1: 6 ATP overstates glycolysis; the net yield is 2.
whyNot.2: About 30–38 ATP is the yield of full aerobic respiration, which needs oxygen.

explain.body: Chloroplasts. Light reactions (thylakoids): chlorophyll captures light, water is split, O₂ released, ATP and NADPH made. Calvin cycle (stroma): CO₂ fixed into sugar using that ATP and NADPH.

test.q: Where in the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place?
test.why: The Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) fixes CO₂ into sugar in the stroma.

whyNot.1: The thylakoid membranes host the light-dependent reactions.
whyNot.2: The mitochondrial matrix hosts the Krebs cycle, part of respiration.
whyNot.3: The cytoplasm hosts glycolysis; the Calvin cycle is inside the chloroplast.
